accounts.prose: This module is the FSM runtime and instance factory. `define` turns a builder callback into one validated, compiled definition shared by independently stateful instances; each instance owns context, current state, a FIFO event queue, timers, identity, and tracing. It exports only `FsmEngine` and its conditional factory type.

referent.description: FSM engine runtime module

qualifications: Apparent behavior from captured TypeScript source; no execution was performed.
The repository README is nearby project documentation and is attributed as intended behavior, not treated as proof.
Dependency coverage is bounded to captured project-owned source requests.

accounts.prose: `define` delegates collection to `FsmBuilderImpl`, then eagerly validates and compiles lookup tables. The builder rejects missing/unknown/unreachable states, duplicate state/event declarations, unknown targets, and transitions placed after an unconditional transition; it records ordered guards/actions plus state-specific and fallback tables. The returned closure reuses that definition while constructing fresh instances and immediately runs initial-state entry actions.

qualifications: Validation and table construction are delegated behavior observed in captured builder source.
Reachability follows external transitions, with fallback targets treated as globally reachable edges.

qualifications: Defines the compiled transition and action-table representation consumed by the runtime.

accounts.prose: `dispatch` always enqueues. The outermost call drains synchronously; re-entrant calls return and remain FIFO. For each event it rejects names absent from the compiled definition, runs state begin actions, tries transitions in declaration order with short-circuiting guards, then tries fallback begins/transitions. A declared transition set whose guards all fail is an implicit handled stay; no state or fallback transition is unhandled. External transitions run exit actions, transition actions, commit state, then entry actions; internal transitions run only transition actions. Any thrown guard/action/error clears queued work and escapes the outer dispatch.

referent.description: event dispatch and transition lifecycle

qualifications: Synchronous behavior is inferred from control flow; host scheduling beyond this call is not assessed.
Action side effects and completed exit actions are not rolled back on failure; state is committed before entry actions but after transition actions.

qualifications: Supplies the ordered transition and action tables traversed by dispatch.

accounts.prose: Actions receive a narrow API that can enqueue events and manage keyed timers. Timer scheduling defaults the key to the event, replaces an existing key, accepts relative delay or `performance.now()` deadline, clamps past/negative times to immediate, and treats `Infinity` as never firing; cancellation delegates wholly to `TimerRegistry`. Apparent defect: timer payload forwarding is reversed—when `payload` exists the engine passes no payload, while payload-less events receive an explicit `undefined`; this conflicts with the action-API type documentation and README’s promised timer payload.

referent.description: action effects and timer delegation

qualifications: The payload discrepancy is a source-level comparison, not a runtime test.
Documentation assertions are attributed to the action-API source and repository README.
Timer registry source includes embedded tests, but they were not executed and do not cover engine payload forwarding.

accounts.prose: `trace` toggles per-instance logging, optionally replaces the logger, resets elapsed-time origin, and returns the instance. Emitted lines combine machine/instance identity, elapsed time, current state/event, fallback status, and guard/action/transition details; unnamed callbacks get ordinal labels.

referent.description: instance tracing

qualifications: Trace formatting uses `performance.now()` and defaults to `console.log`.
Falsy payloads are not rendered because payload output is guarded by a truthiness check.

If no drain is active, that call becomes the outer drain and processes queued items one at a time before returning. If an action dispatches another event while a drain is active, the nested call only appends the event and returns; the new event is processed after the current event has completely finished. Thus an event enqueued by an exit or transition action normally observes the state resulting from the current transition, despite having been requested before the state assignment. If the current processing throws before that queued event is reached, the queue is cleared instead.

referent.description: clarified event dispatch, handler selection, transition ordering, and failure semantics

qualifications: This account clarifies the earlier interpretation rather than correcting it; the implementation independently supports the earlier ordering summary.
“Synchronous” describes the control flow of a call to `dispatch`; timer callbacks and other host scheduling are outside this account.
Queueing prevents recursive event processing, but it does not make dispatch asynchronous: the outermost caller still drains successful re-entrant work before returning.

accounts.prose: For each dequeued item, the engine first asks whether the event occurs anywhere in the compiled definition. If not, it throws the unknown-event error before running begin actions or guards. For a known event, handling has two tiers. It runs the current state’s begin actions, then examines that state’s transitions in declaration order. Guards within one transition are also evaluated in order and stop at the first false result; the first transition whose guards all pass wins. Only if no state transition wins does the engine run fallback begin actions and try fallback transitions in the same fashion. In particular, fallback is attempted not only when the state has no transition, but also when the state has transitions whose guards all reject the event.

referent.description: state-specific then fallback handler selection

qualifications: Begin actions run before transition selection and can therefore have side effects even when every guard later fails or the event ultimately proves unhandled.
A state transition that succeeds prevents fallback begin actions and fallback guards from running.
The ordering described is the ordering of the arrays in the compiled definition; how the builder constructs those arrays was not re-investigated here.

accounts.prose: “Handled” does not necessarily mean that a transition ran. If at least one state-specific or fallback transition was declared for the event, but every candidate fails its guards, the engine records an implicit stay and treats the event as handled: state is unchanged and no transition action runs. By contrast, begin actions alone do not establish handling. If neither tier has any transition for the event, the engine throws the unhandled-event error after any applicable state and fallback begin actions have already run. This differs from an unknown event: an unhandled event is present somewhere in the machine definition, just not transition-handled in the current state or fallback tier.

referent.description: implicit stay and distinction between unknown and unhandled events

qualifications: The implicit stay case requires a nonempty state or fallback transition array; merely having begin actions does not satisfy that test.
The unhandled runtime error captures the machine identifier, current state, event, payload, and the context object; the unknown-event error captures the identifier, event, and payload.
Side effects already performed by begin actions are not rolled back when the engine subsequently throws an unhandled-event error.

accounts.prose: Once a transition wins, an internal transition leaves the state unchanged and runs only its transition actions. An external transition computes its target, runs all source-state exit actions, then all transition actions, assigns the target to the current-state field, and finally runs the target-state entry actions. The assignment therefore is not an atomic boundary with the actions around it. An exception from an exit or transition action occurs before state commitment; an exception from an entry action occurs after commitment. In every case, earlier side effects remain, the pending event queue is discarded by the outer drain, the exception escapes, and the dispatching flag is reset so a later independent call can start a new drain.

referent.description: internal and external transition lifecycle, commit point, and partial failure

qualifications: No rollback mechanism is present for context mutations, external effects, completed actions, timer operations, or a state assignment already made.
Events enqueued by an action are pending work rather than nested processing; they are lost if a later operation in the current drain throws before they are dequeued.

The implementation comment says “Commit state first,” but the executable order assigns the state after exit and transition actions; this account follows the executable statements. No structured inconsistency is reported because the comment is repository text, not an earlier investigram.

accounts.prose: `dispatch` always enqueues. The outermost call drains synchronously; re-entrant calls return and remain FIFO. For each event it rejects names absent from the compiled definition, runs state begin actions, tries transitions in declaration order with short-circuiting guards, then tries fallback begins/transitions. A declared transition set whose guards all fail is an implicit handled stay; no state or fallback transition is unhandled. External transitions run exit actions, transition actions, commit state, then entry actions; internal transitions run only transition actions. Any thrown guard/action/error clears queued work and escapes the outer dispatch.

referent.description: event dispatch and transition lifecycle

qualifications: Synchronous behavior is inferred from control flow; host scheduling beyond this call is not assessed.
Action side effects and completed exit actions are not rolled back on failure; state is committed before entry actions but after transition actions.

accounts.prose: Once a transition wins, an internal transition leaves the state unchanged and runs only its transition actions. An external transition computes its target, runs all source-state exit actions, then all transition actions, assigns the target to the current-state field, and finally runs the target-state entry actions. The assignment therefore is not an atomic boundary with the actions around it. An exception from an exit or transition action occurs before state commitment; an exception from an entry action occurs after commitment. In every case, earlier side effects remain, the pending event queue is discarded by the outer drain, the exception escapes, and the dispatching flag is reset so a later independent call can start a new drain.

accounts.prose: `dispatch` always enqueues. The outermost call drains synchronously; re-entrant calls return and remain FIFO. For each event it rejects names absent from the compiled definition, runs state begin actions, tries transitions in declaration order with short-circuiting guards, then tries fallback begins/transitions. A declared transition set whose guards all fail is an implicit handled stay; no state or fallback transition is unhandled. External transitions run exit actions, transition actions, commit state, then entry actions; internal transitions run only transition actions. Any thrown guard/action/error clears queued work and escapes the outer dispatch.

referent.description: event dispatch and transition lifecycle

qualifications: Synchronous behavior is inferred from control flow; host scheduling beyond this call is not assessed.
Action side effects and completed exit actions are not rolled back on failure; state is committed before entry actions but after transition actions.

accounts.prose: Once a transition wins, an internal transition leaves the state unchanged and runs only its transition actions. An external transition computes its target, runs all source-state exit actions, then all transition actions, assigns the target to the current-state field, and finally runs the target-state entry actions. The assignment therefore is not an atomic boundary with the actions around it. An exception from an exit or transition action occurs before state commitment; an exception from an entry action occurs after commitment. In every case, earlier side effects remain, the pending event queue is discarded by the outer drain, the exception escapes, and the dispatching flag is reset so a later independent call can start a new drain.

accounts.prose: `dispatch` always enqueues. The outermost call drains synchronously; re-entrant calls return and remain FIFO. For each event it rejects names absent from the compiled definition, runs state begin actions, tries transitions in declaration order with short-circuiting guards, then tries fallback begins/transitions. A declared transition set whose guards all fail is an implicit handled stay; no state or fallback transition is unhandled. External transitions run exit actions, transition actions, commit state, then entry actions; internal transitions run only transition actions. Any thrown guard/action/error clears queued work and escapes the outer dispatch.

accounts.prose: Once a transition wins, an internal transition leaves the state unchanged and runs only its transition actions. An external transition computes its target, runs all source-state exit actions, then all transition actions, assigns the target to the current-state field, and finally runs the target-state entry actions. The assignment therefore is not an atomic boundary with the actions around it. An exception from an exit or transition action occurs before state commitment; an exception from an entry action occurs after commitment. In every case, earlier side effects remain, the pending event queue is discarded by the outer drain, the exception escapes, and the dispatching flag is reset so a later independent call can start a new drain.

accounts.prose: The prior account is confirmed and can be sharpened: on an external transition, FsmEngine runs source-state exit actions and transition actions while the source state is still stored, then assigns the target state, and only then invokes target-state entry actions. Consequently, an exception from a target entry action is a post-commit failure: it propagates to the outermost dispatch call, but the machine remains in the target state. This is an explicitly documented runtime semantic as well as the direct ordering in the implementation.

accounts.prose: The commit boundary is narrow and asymmetric. For an external transition, exit actions run first, then transition actions, then `#state = toState`, then target entry actions. Thus guard, exit-action, or transition-action exceptions occur before state assignment and leave the stored state at the source, whereas an entry-action exception occurs after assignment and leaves it at the target. The pre-commit callbacks may nevertheless already have mutated context or produced other side effects.

referent.description: state-assignment boundary relative to transition callbacks

qualifications: The state-persistence distinction follows from statement order and synchronous callback invocation in the captured implementation.
Leaving the stored state unchanged is not equivalent to rolling back callback side effects.

accounts.prose: The outer dispatch catch clears the entire pending event queue for any thrown guard or action, rethrows the same error, and the finally block resets the dispatching flag. Therefore, events enqueued re-entrantly before the failing entry action—including events queued by exit, transition, or earlier entry actions—are discarded rather than processed in the now-committed target state. After unwinding, a later top-level dispatch can start normally and will be handled from that target state.

referent.description: queue and dispatcher state after target-entry failure

qualifications: The statement that a later dispatch starts from the target follows from the target assignment, queue replacement, and `#isDispatching` reset; it was not exercised at runtime here.
Queue clearing does not cancel timers already scheduled through the action API; timer management is separate from the event queue.
The tests directly cover FIFO re-entrant processing and queue clearing after a transition-action exception, but not the post-commit entry-action variant.

accounts.prose: A target entry list is executed in declaration order with `forEach`. If a later entry action throws, earlier target entry actions have already completed; execution stops before subsequent entry actions. No compensating exit of the target, re-entry of the source, context snapshot, timer cancellation, or other rollback path appears in the dispatch error handler. The observable result can therefore be a committed target state with partially applied entry effects.

referent.description: partial entry-action effects without compensation

qualifications: The implementation establishes control-flow ordering, not the nature or reversibility of application-defined side effects.
The absence claim is bounded to the supplied full fsm-engine module; callbacks themselves may implement their own compensation.
The README advises catching errors inside actions, consistent with the engine not supplying transaction semantics.

accounts.prose: `dispatch` always enqueues. The outermost call drains synchronously; re-entrant calls return and remain FIFO. For each event it rejects names absent from the compiled definition, runs state begin actions, tries transitions in declaration order with short-circuiting guards, then tries fallback begins/transitions. A declared transition set whose guards all fail is an implicit handled stay; no state or fallback transition is unhandled. External transitions run exit actions, transition actions, commit state, then entry actions; internal transitions run only transition actions. Any thrown guard/action/error clears queued work and escapes the outer dispatch.

accounts.prose: Once a transition wins, an internal transition leaves the state unchanged and runs only its transition actions. An external transition computes its target, runs all source-state exit actions, then all transition actions, assigns the target to the current-state field, and finally runs the target-state entry actions. The assignment therefore is not an atomic boundary with the actions around it. An exception from an exit or transition action occurs before state commitment; an exception from an entry action occurs after commitment. In every case, earlier side effects remain, the pending event queue is discarded by the outer drain, the exception escapes, and the dispatching flag is reset so a later independent call can start a new drain.

The prior account is confirmed and can be sharpened: on an external transition, FsmEngine runs source-state exit actions and transition actions while the source state is still stored, then assigns the target state, and only then invokes target-state entry actions. Consequently, an exception from a target entry action is a post-commit failure: it propagates to the outermost dispatch call, but the machine remains in the target state. accounts.prose: `dispatch` always enqueues. The outermost call drains synchronously; re-entrant calls return and remain FIFO. For each event it rejects names absent from the compiled definition, runs state begin actions, tries transitions in declaration order with short-circuiting guards, then tries fallback begins/transitions. A declared transition set whose guards all fail is an implicit handled stay; no state or fallback transition is unhandled. External transitions run exit actions, transition actions, commit state, then entry actions; internal transitions run only transition actions. Any thrown guard/action/error clears queued work and escapes the outer dispatch.

referent.description: event dispatch and transition lifecycle

qualifications: Synchronous behavior is inferred from control flow; host scheduling beyond this call is not assessed.
Action side effects and completed exit actions are not rolled back on failure; state is committed before entry actions but after transition actions.

accounts.prose: Once a transition wins, an internal transition leaves the state unchanged and runs only its transition actions. An external transition computes its target, runs all source-state exit actions, then all transition actions, assigns the target to the current-state field, and finally runs the target-state entry actions. The assignment therefore is not an atomic boundary with the actions around it. An exception from an exit or transition action occurs before state commitment; an exception from an entry action occurs after commitment. In every case, earlier side effects remain, the pending event queue is discarded by the outer drain, the exception escapes, and the dispatching flag is reset so a later independent call can start a new drain.

referent.description: internal and external transition lifecycle, commit point, and partial failure

qualifications: No rollback mechanism is present for context mutations, external effects, completed actions, timer operations, or a state assignment already made.
Events enqueued by an action are pending work rather than nested processing; they are lost if a later operation in the current drain throws before they are dequeued.

The implementation comment says “Commit state first,” but the executable order assigns the state after exit and transition actions; this account follows the executable statements. No structured inconsistency is reported because the comment is repository text, not an earlier investigram.

accounts.prose: Once a transition wins, an internal transition leaves the state unchanged and runs only its transition actions. An external transition computes its target, runs all source-state exit actions, then all transition actions, assigns the target to the current-state field, and finally runs the target-state entry actions. The assignment therefore is not an atomic boundary with the actions around it. An exception from an exit or transition action occurs before state commitment; an exception from an entry action occurs after commitment. In every case, earlier side effects remain, the pending event queue is discarded by the outer drain, the exception escapes, and the dispatching flag is reset so a later independent call can start a new drain.

referent.description: internal and external transition lifecycle, commit point, and partial failure

qualifications: No rollback mechanism is present for context mutations, external effects, completed actions, timer operations, or a state assignment already made.
Events enqueued by an action are pending work rather than nested processing; they are lost if a later operation in the current drain throws before they are dequeued.

The implementation comment says “Commit state first,” but the executable order assigns the state after exit and transition actions; this account follows the executable statements. No structured inconsistency is reported because the comment is repository text, not an earlier investigram.

The builder rejects missing/unknown/unreachable states, duplicate state/event declarations, unknown targets, and transitions placed after an unconditional transition; it records ordered guards/actions plus state-specific and fallback tables. The returned closure reuses that definition while constructing fresh instances and immediately runs initial-state entry actions.

accounts.prose: `dispatch` always enqueues. The outermost call drains synchronously; re-entrant calls return and remain FIFO. For each event it rejects names absent from the compiled definition, runs state begin actions, tries transitions in declaration order with short-circuiting guards, then tries fallback begins/transitions. A declared transition set whose guards all fail is an implicit handled stay; no state or fallback transition is unhandled. External transitions run exit actions, transition actions, commit state, then entry actions; internal transitions run only transition actions. Any thrown guard/action/error clears queued work and escapes the outer dispatch.

qualifications: Synchronous behavior is inferred from control flow; host scheduling beyond this call is not assessed.

accounts.prose: Actions receive a narrow API that can enqueue events and manage keyed timers. Timer scheduling defaults the key to the event, replaces an existing key, accepts relative delay or `performance.now()` deadline, clamps past/negative times to immediate, and treats `Infinity` as never firing; cancellation delegates wholly to `TimerRegistry`. Apparent defect: timer payload forwarding is reversed—when `payload` exists the engine passes no payload, while payload-less events receive an explicit `undefined`; this conflicts with the action-API type documentation and README’s promised timer payload.

accounts.prose: `dispatch` always enqueues. The outermost call drains synchronously; re-entrant calls return and remain FIFO. A declared transition set whose guards all fail is an implicit handled stay; no state or fallback transition is unhandled. External transitions run exit actions, transition actions, commit state, then entry actions; internal transitions run only transition actions. Any thrown guard/action/error clears queued work and escapes the outer dispatch.

accounts.prose: Once a transition wins, an internal transition leaves the state unchanged and runs only its transition actions. An external transition computes its target, runs all source-state exit actions, then all transition actions, assigns the target to the current-state field, and finally runs the target-state entry actions. The assignment therefore is not an atomic boundary with the actions around it. An exception from an exit or transition action occurs before state commitment; an exception from an entry action occurs after commitment. In every case, earlier side effects remain, the pending event queue is discarded by the outer drain, the exception escapes, and the dispatching flag is reset so a later independent call can start a new drain.

@investigram-a6f543c9 · interpretation
`define` delegates collection to `FsmBuilderImpl`, then eagerly validates and compiles lookup tables. The builder rejects missing/unknown/unreachable states, duplicate state/event declarations, unknown targets, and transitions placed after an unconditional transition; it records ordered guards/actions plus state-specific and fallback tables. The returned closure reuses that definition while constructing fresh instances and immediately runs initial-state entry actions.
Referent: definition, validation, compilation, and instantiation
  Qualification: Validation and table construction are delegated behavior observed in captured builder source.
  Qualification: Reachability follows external transitions, with fallback targets treated as globally reachable edges.

@investigram-04d79256 · interpretation
`dispatch` always enqueues. The outermost call drains synchronously; re-entrant calls return and remain FIFO. For each event it rejects names absent from the compiled definition, runs state begin actions, tries transitions in declaration order with short-circuiting guards, then tries fallback begins/transitions. A declared transition set whose guards all fail is an implicit handled stay; no state or fallback transition is unhandled. External transitions run exit actions, transition actions, commit state, then entry actions; internal transitions run only transition actions. Any thrown guard/action/error clears queued work and escapes the outer dispatch.
Referent: event dispatch and transition lifecycle
  Qualification: Synchronous behavior is inferred from control flow; host scheduling beyond this call is not assessed.
  Qualification: Action side effects and completed exit actions are not rolled back on failure; state is committed before entry actions but after transition actions.

@investigram-300a00e5 · interpretation
Actions receive a narrow API that can enqueue events and manage keyed timers. Timer scheduling defaults the key to the event, replaces an existing key, accepts relative delay or `performance.now()` deadline, clamps past/negative times to immediate, and treats `Infinity` as never firing; cancellation delegates wholly to `TimerRegistry`. Apparent defect: timer payload forwarding is reversed—when `payload` exists the engine passes no payload, while payload-less events receive an explicit `undefined`; this conflicts with the action-API type documentation and README’s promised timer payload.
Referent: action effects and timer delegation
  Qualification: The payload discrepancy is a source-level comparison, not a runtime test.
  Qualification: Documentation assertions are attributed to the action-API source and repository README.
  Qualification: Timer registry source includes embedded tests, but they were not executed and do not cover engine payload forwarding.

accounts.prose: `dispatch` always enqueues. The outermost call drains synchronously; re-entrant calls return and remain FIFO. For each event it rejects names absent from the compiled definition, runs state begin actions, tries transitions in declaration order with short-circuiting guards, then tries fallback begins/transitions. A declared transition set whose guards all fail is an implicit handled stay; no state or fallback transition is unhandled. External transitions run exit actions, transition actions, commit state, then entry actions; internal transitions run only transition actions. Any thrown guard/action/error clears queued work and escapes the outer dispatch.

referent.description: event dispatch and transition lifecycle

qualifications: Synchronous behavior is inferred from control flow; host scheduling beyond this call is not assessed.
Action side effects and completed exit actions are not rolled back on failure; state is committed before entry actions but after transition actions.

accounts.prose: `dispatch` always enqueues. The outermost call drains synchronously; re-entrant calls return and remain FIFO. For each event it rejects names absent from the compiled definition, runs state begin actions, tries transitions in declaration order with short-circuiting guards, then tries fallback begins/transitions. A declared transition set whose guards all fail is an implicit handled stay; no state or fallback transition is unhandled. External transitions run exit actions, transition actions, commit state, then entry actions; internal transitions run only transition actions. Any thrown guard/action/error clears queued work and escapes the outer dispatch.

qualifications: Synchronous behavior is inferred from control flow; host scheduling beyond this call is not assessed.
Action side effects and completed exit actions are not rolled back on failure; state is committed before entry actions but after transition actions.

accounts.prose: Once a transition wins, an internal transition leaves the state unchanged and runs only its transition actions. An external transition computes its target, runs all source-state exit actions, then all transition actions, assigns the target to the current-state field, and finally runs the target-state entry actions. The assignment therefore is not an atomic boundary with the actions around it. An exception from an exit or transition action occurs before state commitment; an exception from an entry action occurs after commitment. In every case, earlier side effects remain, the pending event queue is discarded by the outer drain, the exception escapes, and the dispatching flag is reset so a later independent call can start a new drain.

referent.description: internal and external transition lifecycle, commit point, and partial failure

qualifications: No rollback mechanism is present for context mutations, external effects, completed actions, timer operations, or a state assignment already made.
Events enqueued by an action are pending work rather than nested processing; they are lost if a later operation in the current drain throws before they are dequeued.

The implementation comment says “Commit state first,” but the executable order assigns the state after exit and transition actions; this account follows the executable statements. No structured inconsistency is reported because the comment is repository text, not an earlier investigram.

accounts.prose: `dispatch` is best understood as a synchronous queue drain, not as a direct recursive event handler. Every call first appends `{event, payload}` to the instance’s FIFO queue. If no drain is active, that call becomes the outer drain and processes queued items one at a time before returning. If an action dispatches another event while a drain is active, the nested call only appends the event and returns; the new event is processed after the current event has completely finished. Thus an event enqueued by an exit or transition action normally observes the state resulting from the current transition, despite having been requested before the state assignment. If the current processing throws before that queued event is reached, the queue is cleared instead.

referent.description: clarified event dispatch, handler selection, transition ordering, and failure semantics

qualifications: This account clarifies the earlier interpretation rather than correcting it; the implementation independently supports the earlier ordering summary.
“Synchronous” describes the control flow of a call to `dispatch`; timer callbacks and other host scheduling are outside this account.
Queueing prevents recursive event processing, but it does not make dispatch asynchronous: the outermost caller still drains successful re-entrant work before returning.

accounts.prose: For each dequeued item, the engine first asks whether the event occurs anywhere in the compiled definition. If not, it throws the unknown-event error before running begin actions or guards. For a known event, handling has two tiers. It runs the current state’s begin actions, then examines that state’s transitions in declaration order. Guards within one transition are also evaluated in order and stop at the first false result; the first transition whose guards all pass wins. Only if no state transition wins does the engine run fallback begin actions and try fallback transitions in the same fashion. In particular, fallback is attempted not only when the state has no transition, but also when the state has transitions whose guards all reject the event.

referent.description: state-specific then fallback handler selection

qualifications: Begin actions run before transition selection and can therefore have side effects even when every guard later fails or the event ultimately proves unhandled.
A state transition that succeeds prevents fallback begin actions and fallback guards from running.
The ordering described is the ordering of the arrays in the compiled definition; how the builder constructs those arrays was not re-investigated here.

accounts.prose: “Handled” does not necessarily mean that a transition ran. If at least one state-specific or fallback transition was declared for the event, but every candidate fails its guards, the engine records an implicit stay and treats the event as handled: state is unchanged and no transition action runs. By contrast, begin actions alone do not establish handling. If neither tier has any transition for the event, the engine throws the unhandled-event error after any applicable state and fallback begin actions have already run. This differs from an unknown event: an unhandled event is present somewhere in the machine definition, just not transition-handled in the current state or fallback tier.

referent.description: implicit stay and distinction between unknown and unhandled events

qualifications: The implicit stay case requires a nonempty state or fallback transition array; merely having begin actions does not satisfy that test.
The unhandled runtime error captures the machine identifier, current state, event, payload, and the context object; the unknown-event error captures the identifier, event, and payload.
Side effects already performed by begin actions are not rolled back when the engine subsequently throws an unhandled-event error.

accounts.prose: `dispatch` always enqueues. The outermost call drains synchronously; re-entrant calls return and remain FIFO. External transitions run exit actions, transition actions, commit state, then entry actions; internal transitions run only transition actions. Any thrown guard/action/error clears queued work and escapes the outer dispatch.

accounts.prose: `dispatch` always enqueues. The outermost call drains synchronously; re-entrant calls return and remain FIFO. For each event it rejects names absent from the compiled definition, runs state begin actions, tries transitions in declaration order with short-circuiting guards, then tries fallback begins/transitions. A declared transition set whose guards all fail is an implicit handled stay; no state or fallback transition is unhandled. External transitions run exit actions, transition actions, commit state, then entry actions; internal transitions run only transition actions. Any thrown guard/action/error clears queued work and escapes the outer dispatch.

referent.description: event dispatch and transition lifecycle

qualifications: Synchronous behavior is inferred from control flow; host scheduling beyond this call is not assessed.
Action side effects and completed exit actions are not rolled back on failure; state is committed before entry actions but after transition actions.

accounts.prose: Once a transition wins, an internal transition leaves the state unchanged and runs only its transition actions. An external transition computes its target, runs all source-state exit actions, then all transition actions, assigns the target to the current-state field, and finally runs the target-state entry actions. The assignment therefore is not an atomic boundary with the actions around it. An exception from an exit or transition action occurs before state commitment; an exception from an entry action occurs after commitment. In every case, earlier side effects remain, the pending event queue is discarded by the outer drain, the exception escapes, and the dispatching flag is reset so a later independent call can start a new drain.

@investigram-a86b8e57 · interpretation
`dispatch` is best understood as a synchronous queue drain, not as a direct recursive event handler. Every call first appends `{event, payload}` to the instance’s FIFO queue. If no drain is active, that call becomes the outer drain and processes queued items one at a time before returning. If an action dispatches another event while a drain is active, the nested call only appends the event and returns; the new event is processed after the current event has completely finished. Thus an event enqueued by an exit or transition action normally observes the state resulting from the current transition, despite having been requested before the state assignment. If the current processing throws before that queued event is reached, the queue is cleared instead.
Referent: clarified event dispatch, handler selection, transition ordering, and failure semantics
  Qualification: This account clarifies the earlier interpretation rather than correcting it; the implementation independently supports the earlier ordering summary.
  Qualification: “Synchronous” describes the control flow of a call to `dispatch`; timer callbacks and other host scheduling are outside this account.
  Qualification: Queueing prevents recursive event processing, but it does not make dispatch asynchronous: the outermost caller still drains successful re-entrant work before returning.

@investigram-70695d40 · interpretation
For each dequeued item, the engine first asks whether the event occurs anywhere in the compiled definition. If not, it throws the unknown-event error before running begin actions or guards. For a known event, handling has two tiers. It runs the current state’s begin actions, then examines that state’s transitions in declaration order. Guards within one transition are also evaluated in order and stop at the first false result; the first transition whose guards all pass wins. Only if no state transition wins does the engine run fallback begin actions and try fallback transitions in the same fashion. In particular, fallback is attempted not only when the state has no transition, but also when the state has transitions whose guards all reject the event.
Referent: state-specific then fallback handler selection
  Qualification: Begin actions run before transition selection and can therefore have side effects even when every guard later fails or the event ultimately proves unhandled.
  Qualification: A state transition that succeeds prevents fallback begin actions and fallback guards from running.
  Qualification: The ordering described is the ordering of the arrays in the compiled definition; how the builder constructs those arrays was not re-investigated here.

@investigram-7472008d · interpretation
“Handled” does not necessarily mean that a transition ran. If at least one state-specific or fallback transition was declared for the event, but every candidate fails its guards, the engine records an implicit stay and treats the event as handled: state is unchanged and no transition action runs. By contrast, begin actions alone do not establish handling. If neither tier has any transition for the event, the engine throws the unhandled-event error after any applicable state and fallback begin actions have already run. This differs from an unknown event: an unhandled event is present somewhere in the machine definition, just not transition-handled in the current state or fallback tier.

@investigram-a17803e1 · interpretation
Once a transition wins, an internal transition leaves the state unchanged and runs only its transition actions. An external transition computes its target, runs all source-state exit actions, then all transition actions, assigns the target to the current-state field, and finally runs the target-state entry actions. The assignment therefore is not an atomic boundary with the actions around it. An exception from an exit or transition action occurs before state commitment; an exception from an entry action occurs after commitment. In every case, earlier side effects remain, the pending event queue is discarded by the outer drain, the exception escapes, and the dispatching flag is reset so a later independent call can start a new drain.

accounts.prose: `dispatch` is best understood as a synchronous queue drain, not as a direct recursive event handler. Every call first appends `{event, payload}` to the instance’s FIFO queue. If no drain is active, that call becomes the outer drain and processes queued items one at a time before returning. If an action dispatches another event while a drain is active, the nested call only appends the event and returns; the new event is processed after the current event has completely finished. Thus an event enqueued by an exit or transition action normally observes the state resulting from the current transition, despite having been requested before the state assignment. If the current processing throws before that queued event is reached, the queue is cleared instead.

referent.description: clarified event dispatch, handler selection, transition ordering, and failure semantics

qualifications: This account clarifies the earlier interpretation rather than correcting it; the implementation independently supports the earlier ordering summary.
“Synchronous” describes the control flow of a call to `dispatch`; timer callbacks and other host scheduling are outside this account.
Queueing prevents recursive event processing, but it does not make dispatch asynchronous: the outermost caller still drains successful re-entrant work before returning.

accounts.prose: For each dequeued item, the engine first asks whether the event occurs anywhere in the compiled definition. If not, it throws the unknown-event error before running begin actions or guards. For a known event, handling has two tiers. It runs the current state’s begin actions, then examines that state’s transitions in declaration order. Guards within one transition are also evaluated in order and stop at the first false result; the first transition whose guards all pass wins. Only if no state transition wins does the engine run fallback begin actions and try fallback transitions in the same fashion. In particular, fallback is attempted not only when the state has no transition, but also when the state has transitions whose guards all reject the event.

referent.description: state-specific then fallback handler selection

qualifications: Begin actions run before transition selection and can therefore have side effects even when every guard later fails or the event ultimately proves unhandled.
A state transition that succeeds prevents fallback begin actions and fallback guards from running.
The ordering described is the ordering of the arrays in the compiled definition; how the builder constructs those arrays was not re-investigated here.

accounts.prose: “Handled” does not necessarily mean that a transition ran. If at least one state-specific or fallback transition was declared for the event, but every candidate fails its guards, the engine records an implicit stay and treats the event as handled: state is unchanged and no transition action runs. By contrast, begin actions alone do not establish handling. If neither tier has any transition for the event, the engine throws the unhandled-event error after any applicable state and fallback begin actions have already run. This differs from an unknown event: an unhandled event is present somewhere in the machine definition, just not transition-handled in the current state or fallback tier.

referent.description: implicit stay and distinction between unknown and unhandled events

qualifications: The implicit stay case requires a nonempty state or fallback transition array; merely having begin actions does not satisfy that test.
The unhandled runtime error captures the machine identifier, current state, event, payload, and the context object; the unknown-event error captures the identifier, event, and payload.
Side effects already performed by begin actions are not rolled back when the engine subsequently throws an unhandled-event error.

@investigram-a86b8e57 · interpretation
`dispatch` is best understood as a synchronous queue drain, not as a direct recursive event handler. Every call first appends `{event, payload}` to the instance’s FIFO queue. If no drain is active, that call becomes the outer drain and processes queued items one at a time before returning. If an action dispatches another event while a drain is active, the nested call only appends the event and returns; the new event is processed after the current event has completely finished. Thus an event enqueued by an exit or transition action normally observes the state resulting from the current transition, despite having been requested before the state assignment. If the current processing throws before that queued event is reached, the queue is cleared instead.
Referent: clarified event dispatch, handler selection, transition ordering, and failure semantics
  Qualification: This account clarifies the earlier interpretation rather than correcting it; the implementation independently supports the earlier ordering summary.
  Qualification: “Synchronous” describes the control flow of a call to `dispatch`; timer callbacks and other host scheduling are outside this account.
  Qualification: Queueing prevents recursive event processing, but it does not make dispatch asynchronous: the outermost caller still drains successful re-entrant work before returning.

@investigram-70695d40 · interpretation
For each dequeued item, the engine first asks whether the event occurs anywhere in the compiled definition. If not, it throws the unknown-event error before running begin actions or guards. For a known event, handling has two tiers. It runs the current state’s begin actions, then examines that state’s transitions in declaration order. Guards within one transition are also evaluated in order and stop at the first false result; the first transition whose guards all pass wins. Only if no state transition wins does the engine run fallback begin actions and try fallback transitions in the same fashion. In particular, fallback is attempted not only when the state has no transition, but also when the state has transitions whose guards all reject the event.
Referent: state-specific then fallback handler selection
  Qualification: Begin actions run before transition selection and can therefore have side effects even when every guard later fails or the event ultimately proves unhandled.
  Qualification: A state transition that succeeds prevents fallback begin actions and fallback guards from running.
  Qualification: The ordering described is the ordering of the arrays in the compiled definition; how the builder constructs those arrays was not re-investigated here.

@investigram-7472008d · interpretation
“Handled” does not necessarily mean that a transition ran. If at least one state-specific or fallback transition was declared for the event, but every candidate fails its guards, the engine records an implicit stay and treats the event as handled: state is unchanged and no transition action runs. By contrast, begin actions alone do not establish handling. If neither tier has any transition for the event, the engine throws the unhandled-event error after any applicable state and fallback begin actions have already run. This differs from an unknown event: an unhandled event is present somewhere in the machine definition, just not transition-handled in the current state or fallback tier.
Referent: implicit stay and distinction between unknown and unhandled events
  Qualification: The implicit stay case requires a nonempty state or fallback transition array; merely having begin actions does not satisfy that test.
  Qualification: The unhandled runtime error captures the machine identifier, current state, event, payload, and the context object; the unknown-event error captures the identifier, event, and payload.
  Qualification: Side effects already performed by begin actions are not rolled back when the engine subsequently throws an unhandled-event error.

@investigram-a17803e1 · interpretation
Once a transition wins, an internal transition leaves the state unchanged and runs only its transition actions. An external transition computes its target, runs all source-state exit actions, then all transition actions, assigns the target to the current-state field, and finally runs the target-state entry actions. The assignment therefore is not an atomic boundary with the actions around it. An exception from an exit or transition action occurs before state commitment; an exception from an entry action occurs after commitment. In every case, earlier side effects remain, the pending event queue is discarded by the outer drain, the exception escapes, and the dispatching flag is reset so a later independent call can start a new drain.
Referent: internal and external transition lifecycle, commit point, and partial failure
  Qualification: No rollback mechanism is present for context mutations, external effects, completed actions, timer operations, or a state assignment already made.
  Qualification: Events enqueued by an action are pending work rather than nested processing; they are lost if a later operation in the current drain throws before they are dequeued.
  Qualification: The implementation comment says “Commit state first,” but the executable order assigns the state after exit and transition actions; this account follows the executable statements. No structured inconsistency is reported because the comment is repository text, not an earlier investigram.

accounts.prose: `dispatch` always enqueues. The outermost call drains synchronously; re-entrant calls return and remain FIFO. For each event it rejects names absent from the compiled definition, runs state begin actions, tries transitions in declaration order with short-circuiting guards, then tries fallback begins/transitions. A declared transition set whose guards all fail is an implicit handled stay; no state or fallback transition is unhandled. External transitions run exit actions, transition actions, commit state, then entry actions; internal transitions run only transition actions. Any thrown guard/action/error clears queued work and escapes the outer dispatch.

referent.description: event dispatch and transition lifecycle

qualifications: Synchronous behavior is inferred from control flow; host scheduling beyond this call is not assessed.
Action side effects and completed exit actions are not rolled back on failure; state is committed before entry actions but after transition actions.

accounts.prose: Once a transition wins, an internal transition leaves the state unchanged and runs only its transition actions. An external transition computes its target, runs all source-state exit actions, then all transition actions, assigns the target to the current-state field, and finally runs the target-state entry actions. The assignment therefore is not an atomic boundary with the actions around it. An exception from an exit or transition action occurs before state commitment; an exception from an entry action occurs after commitment. In every case, earlier side effects remain, the pending event queue is discarded by the outer drain, the exception escapes, and the dispatching flag is reset so a later independent call can start a new drain.

referent.description: internal and external transition lifecycle, commit point, and partial failure

accounts.prose: `define` delegates collection to `FsmBuilderImpl`, then eagerly validates and compiles lookup tables. The builder rejects missing/unknown/unreachable states, duplicate state/event declarations, unknown targets, and transitions placed after an unconditional transition; it records ordered guards/actions plus state-specific and fallback tables. The returned closure reuses that definition while constructing fresh instances and immediately runs initial-state entry actions.

qualifications: Validation and table construction are delegated behavior observed in captured builder source.

accounts.prose: `dispatch` always enqueues. The outermost call drains synchronously; re-entrant calls return and remain FIFO. For each event it rejects names absent from the compiled definition, runs state begin actions, tries transitions in declaration order with short-circuiting guards, then tries fallback begins/transitions. A declared transition set whose guards all fail is an implicit handled stay; no state or fallback transition is unhandled. External transitions run exit actions, transition actions, commit state, then entry actions; internal transitions run only transition actions. Any thrown guard/action/error clears queued work and escapes the outer dispatch.

referent.description: event dispatch and transition lifecycle

qualifications: Synchronous behavior is inferred from control flow; host scheduling beyond this call is not assessed.
Action side effects and completed exit actions are not rolled back on failure; state is committed before entry actions but after transition actions.

accounts.prose: Actions receive a narrow API that can enqueue events and manage keyed timers. Timer scheduling defaults the key to the event, replaces an existing key, accepts relative delay or `performance.now()` deadline, clamps past/negative times to immediate, and treats `Infinity` as never firing; cancellation delegates wholly to `TimerRegistry`. Apparent defect: timer payload forwarding is reversed—when `payload` exists the engine passes no payload, while payload-less events receive an explicit `undefined`; this conflicts with the action-API type documentation and README’s promised timer payload.

referent.description: action effects and timer delegation

qualifications: The payload discrepancy is a source-level comparison, not a runtime test.

accounts.prose: `dispatch` always enqueues. The outermost call drains synchronously; re-entrant calls return and remain FIFO. For each event it rejects names absent from the compiled definition, runs state begin actions, tries transitions in declaration order with short-circuiting guards, then tries fallback begins/transitions. A declared transition set whose guards all fail is an implicit handled stay; no state or fallback transition is unhandled. External transitions run exit actions, transition actions, commit state, then entry actions; internal transitions run only transition actions. Any thrown guard/action/error clears queued work and escapes the outer dispatch.

referent.description: event dispatch and transition lifecycle

qualifications: Synchronous behavior is inferred from control flow; host scheduling beyond this call is not assessed.
Action side effects and completed exit actions are not rolled back on failure; state is committed before entry actions but after transition actions.

accounts.prose: Once a transition wins, an internal transition leaves the state unchanged and runs only its transition actions. An external transition computes its target, runs all source-state exit actions, then all transition actions, assigns the target to the current-state field, and finally runs the target-state entry actions. The assignment therefore is not an atomic boundary with the actions around it. An exception from an exit or transition action occurs before state commitment; an exception from an entry action occurs after commitment. In every case, earlier side effects remain, the pending event queue is discarded by the outer drain, the exception escapes, and the dispatching flag is reset so a later independent call can start a new drain.

referent.description: internal and external transition lifecycle, commit point, and partial failure

qualifications: No rollback mechanism is present for context mutations, external effects, completed actions, timer operations, or a state assignment already made.
Events enqueued by an action are pending work rather than nested processing; they are lost if a later operation in the current drain throws before they are dequeued.

@investigram-04d79256 · interpretation
`dispatch` always enqueues. The outermost call drains synchronously; re-entrant calls return and remain FIFO. accounts.prose: Once a transition wins, an internal transition leaves the state unchanged and runs only its transition actions. An external transition computes its target, runs all source-state exit actions, then all transition actions, assigns the target to the current-state field, and finally runs the target-state entry actions. The assignment therefore is not an atomic boundary with the actions around it. An exception from an exit or transition action occurs before state commitment; an exception from an entry action occurs after commitment. In every case, earlier side effects remain, the pending event queue is discarded by the outer drain, the exception escapes, and the dispatching flag is reset so a later independent call can start a new drain.

referent.description: internal and external transition lifecycle, commit point, and partial failure

accounts.prose: `dispatch` always enqueues. The outermost call drains synchronously; re-entrant calls return and remain FIFO. For each event it rejects names absent from the compiled definition, runs state begin actions, tries transitions in declaration order with short-circuiting guards, then tries fallback begins/transitions. A declared transition set whose guards all fail is an implicit handled stay; no state or fallback transition is unhandled. External transitions run exit actions, transition actions, commit state, then entry actions; internal transitions run only transition actions. Any thrown guard/action/error clears queued work and escapes the outer dispatch.

accounts.prose: Once a transition wins, an internal transition leaves the state unchanged and runs only its transition actions. An external transition computes its target, runs all source-state exit actions, then all transition actions, assigns the target to the current-state field, and finally runs the target-state entry actions. The assignment therefore is not an atomic boundary with the actions around it. An exception from an exit or transition action occurs before state commitment; an exception from an entry action occurs after commitment. In every case, earlier side effects remain, the pending event queue is discarded by the outer drain, the exception escapes, and the dispatching flag is reset so a later independent call can start a new drain.

qualifications: No rollback mechanism is present for context mutations, external effects, completed actions, timer operations, or a state assignment already made.
Events enqueued by an action are pending work rather than nested processing; they are lost if a later operation in the current drain throws before they are dequeued.

accounts.prose: `dispatch` always enqueues. The outermost call drains synchronously; re-entrant calls return and remain FIFO. For each event it rejects names absent from the compiled definition, runs state begin actions, tries transitions in declaration order with short-circuiting guards, then tries fallback begins/transitions. A declared transition set whose guards all fail is an implicit handled stay; no state or fallback transition is unhandled. External transitions run exit actions, transition actions, commit state, then entry actions; internal transitions run only transition actions. Any thrown guard/action/error clears queued work and escapes the outer dispatch.

referent.description: event dispatch and transition lifecycle

qualifications: Synchronous behavior is inferred from control flow; host scheduling beyond this call is not assessed.
Action side effects and completed exit actions are not rolled back on failure; state is committed before entry actions but after transition actions.

accounts.prose: Once a transition wins, an internal transition leaves the state unchanged and runs only its transition actions. An external transition computes its target, runs all source-state exit actions, then all transition actions, assigns the target to the current-state field, and finally runs the target-state entry actions. The assignment therefore is not an atomic boundary with the actions around it. An exception from an exit or transition action occurs before state commitment; an exception from an entry action occurs after commitment. In every case, earlier side effects remain, the pending event queue is discarded by the outer drain, the exception escapes, and the dispatching flag is reset so a later independent call can start a new drain.

qualifications: No rollback mechanism is present for context mutations, external effects, completed actions, timer operations, or a state assignment already made.
Events enqueued by an action are pending work rather than nested processing; they are lost if a later operation in the current drain throws before they are dequeued.

accounts.prose: `dispatch` always enqueues. The outermost call drains synchronously; re-entrant calls return and remain FIFO. For each event it rejects names absent from the compiled definition, runs state begin actions, tries transitions in declaration order with short-circuiting guards, then tries fallback begins/transitions. A declared transition set whose guards all fail is an implicit handled stay; no state or fallback transition is unhandled. External transitions run exit actions, transition actions, commit state, then entry actions; internal transitions run only transition actions. Any thrown guard/action/error clears queued work and escapes the outer dispatch.

referent.description: event dispatch and transition lifecycle

qualifications: Synchronous behavior is inferred from control flow; host scheduling beyond this call is not assessed.
Action side effects and completed exit actions are not rolled back on failure; state is committed before entry actions but after transition actions.

accounts.prose: Once a transition wins, an internal transition leaves the state unchanged and runs only its transition actions. An external transition computes its target, runs all source-state exit actions, then all transition actions, assigns the target to the current-state field, and finally runs the target-state entry actions. The assignment therefore is not an atomic boundary with the actions around it. An exception from an exit or transition action occurs before state commitment; an exception from an entry action occurs after commitment. In every case, earlier side effects remain, the pending event queue is discarded by the outer drain, the exception escapes, and the dispatching flag is reset so a later independent call can start a new drain.

referent.description: internal and external transition lifecycle, commit point, and partial failure

qualifications: No rollback mechanism is present for context mutations, external effects, completed actions, timer operations, or a state assignment already made.
Events enqueued by an action are pending work rather than nested processing; they are lost if a later operation in the current drain throws before they are dequeued.

The implementation comment says “Commit state first,” but the executable order assigns the state after exit and transition actions; this account follows the executable statements. No structured inconsistency is reported because the comment is repository text, not an earlier investigram.

An external transition computes its target, runs all source-state exit actions, then all transition actions, assigns the target to the current-state field, and finally runs the target-state entry actions. The assignment therefore is not an atomic boundary with the actions around it. An exception from an exit or transition action occurs before state commitment; an exception from an entry action occurs after commitment. In every case, earlier side effects remain, the pending event queue is discarded by the outer drain, the exception escapes, and the dispatching flag is reset so a later independent call can start a new drain.

referent.description: internal and external transition lifecycle, commit point, and partial failure

qualifications: No rollback mechanism is present for context mutations, external effects, completed actions, timer operations, or a state assignment already made.
Events enqueued by an action are pending work rather than nested processing; they are lost if a later operation in the current drain throws before they are dequeued.

The implementation comment says “Commit state first,” but the executable order assigns the state after exit and transition actions; this account follows the executable statements. No structured inconsistency is reported because the comment is repository text, not an earlier investigram.
